content: Infants born prematurely are at an increased risk of developing early hypernatraemia, which refers to elevated sodium levels in the blood, and late hyponatraemia, which refers to abnormally low sodium levels. Concerns exist that imbalances in sodium intake may influence neonatal complications, growth, and developmental outcomes. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of higher versus lower sodium supplementation in preterm infants. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and trial registries, and reviewed reference lists of relevant studies. They analyzed the effects of sodium supplementation provided early (within the first 7 days after birth), late (7 days or more after birth), and during both early and late periods. The review included randomized, quasi-randomized, or cluster-randomized controlled trials that compared higher versus lower sodium supplementation in preterm infants. Eligible participants were infants born before 37 weeks of gestation or with a birth weight below 2500 grams. Studies with predetermined differences in water intake between groups were excluded. Data were independently assessed by two reviewers, and the certainty of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. Nine studies were included in the review, but data could not be extracted from one study involving 20 infants. Eight studies, involving 241 infants, were included in the quantitative meta-analysis. Four studies (103 infants) compared early higher versus lower sodium intake, and four studies (138 infants) compared late higher versus lower sodium intake. Two studies (103 infants) compared intermediate sodium supplementation (3 to <5 mmol/kg/day) versus no supplementation, and two studies (52 infants) compared higher sodium supplementation (≥5 mmol/kg/day) versus no supplementation. Only two studies (63 infants) were assessed as having a low risk of bias. Early Sodium Supplementation (Within 7 Days of Birth) Higher sodium intake during the early period may not significantly affect mortality (risk ratio [RR] 1.02, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.38 to 2.72; low-certainty evidence). Neurodevelopmental outcomes were not reported in the studies. Early higher sodium intake may result in a similar incidence of hyponatraemia (sodium <130 mmol/L) compared to lower intake (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.40 to 1.13; low-certainty evidence). However, early higher sodium intake may increase the incidence of hypernatraemia (sodium ≥150 mmol/L) (RR 1.62, 95% CI 1.00 to 2.65; risk difference [RD] 0.17, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.34; number needed to treat for harm = 6; low-certainty evidence). Postnatal growth failure was not reported in the studies. The evidence is very uncertain regarding the effect of early higher sodium intake on necrotising enterocolitis (RR 4.60, 95% CI 0.23 to 90.84; very low-certainty evidence). Chronic lung disease at 36 weeks was not reported. Late Sodium Supplementation (7 Days or More After Birth) Higher sodium intake during the late period may not significantly affect mortality (RR 0.13, 95% CI 0.01 to 2.20; very low-certainty evidence). Neurodevelopmental outcomes were not reported in the studies. Late higher sodium intake may reduce the incidence of hyponatraemia (sodium <130 mmol/L) (RR 0.13, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.50; RD −0.42, 95% CI −0.59 to −0.24; number needed to treat for benefit = 2; low-certainty evidence). The evidence is very uncertain regarding the effect of late higher sodium intake on hypernatraemia (sodium ≥150 mmol/L) (RR 7.88, 95% CI 0.43 to 144.81; very low-certainty evidence). A single small study suggested that late higher sodium intake may reduce the incidence of postnatal growth failure (RR 0.25, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.69; low-certainty evidence). The evidence is very uncertain regarding the effect of late higher sodium intake on necrotising enterocolitis (RR 0.07, 95% CI 0.00 to 1.25; very low-certainty evidence) and chronic lung disease (RR 2.03, 95% CI 0.80 to 5.20; very low-certainty evidence). Combined Early and Late Sodium Supplementation (Day 1 to 28 After Birth) Combined early and late higher sodium supplementation may not significantly affect the incidence of hypernatraemia (sodium ≥150 mmol/L) (RR 2.50, 95% CI 0.63 to 10.00; very low-certainty evidence). No other outcomes were reported for this comparison. Authors' Conclusions Early higher sodium supplementation (within 7 days of birth) may increase the risk of hypernatraemia but may result in a similar incidence of hyponatraemia compared to lower supplementation. The effects on mortality, neonatal complications, growth, and long-term developmental outcomes remain uncertain due to limited evidence. Late higher sodium supplementation (7 days or more after birth) may reduce the incidence of hyponatraemia and may reduce postnatal growth failure. However, the effects on hypernatraemia, mortality, other neonatal complications, and long-term developmental outcomes are uncertain. The evidence is insufficient to determine the effects of combined early and late higher sodium supplementation on outcomes.
